connections.why: Watson and Crick's pairing suggested that each strand of the double helix is the template for a new partner; Meselson and Stahl's heavy-nitrogen bands showed in 1958 that every copy does keep one old strand.
The experiment rests on what the neutron explained: nitrogen-15 carries one more neutron than nitrogen-14, behaves the same in the cell's chemistry, and so marks DNA by weight alone.
PCR copies DNA by the scheme Meselson and Stahl demonstrated: heat parts the two strands and DNA polymerase builds a new partner on each.
The experiment was done at Caltech, where Feynman sat on Meselson's dissertation committee, the kind of conversation across biology and physics that drew him there.
In June 1960 Brenner and Jacob used Meselson's ultracentrifuge at Caltech to show that a phage's new RNA ran on the cell's old ribosomes, part of the finding of messenger RNA.

Meselson heard Nirenberg read the poly-U result to about two dozen people in Moscow in August 1961 and fetched Crick, who gave Nirenberg the stage of his symposium before an audience of about a thousand.
